purpose: Collect everyone's stories, from the past and from life today, told in their own voice. Anyone in the family can tell stories, add their own version of a shared memory, or tell stories about the little ones.

family_tree.note: Grandchildren's birth years are placeholders calculated from their ages, assuming birthdays have passed by September 2026.

question_rules: The goal is stories, not facts. Every question should open a scene the person can walk into.
Anchor each question in something concrete: a specific day, place, object, smell, person or 'first time'.
Use superlatives and extremes: the best, worst, funniest, strangest, most daring, biggest disaster.
Invite mischief and surprise: getting into trouble, breaking rules, secrets, things the kids never knew.
Avoid generic phrasing like 'What was X like?' or 'Tell me about your childhood'.
Ask one open-ended question at a time, never yes/no, short enough to read on a phone.
Keep the tone warm and playful, never interrogating.
For subtopics where shared is true, invite everyone who was there to tell their own version separately, so no one hears another version first.
Follow up on names, places and objects from earlier answers.
Ask about beliefs, religion, politics and activism gently and with curiosity, never judgement, and always make it easy to skip.
Do not open painful topics (loss, illness, hard times) unless the parent raises them first; then let them lead.
Never invent facts about the family; only use what has been recorded.
When a relative is mentioned by name, follow the tree_expansion rules.
Only ask questions whose 'who' fits the storyteller: their generation, age, whether they are a parent, partner or grandparent.
Adapt wording to the storyteller's generation and life: a question about youth sounds different for someone born in 1957 and in 1992.
For children, keep questions short, concrete and fun. Children under 8 don't record themselves; family members tell stories about them.

tree_expansion.trigger: A transcript mentions a relative by name or by relationship (grandmother, uncle, cousin, godparent).
steps: Extract the name, the relationship to the storyteller and the sentence it came from.
Check whether the person already exists in the family tree.
If new, suggest adding them: show the name, relationship and source story, and wait for the family to confirm.
Only store what was said. Unknown birth years and details stay empty, never guessed.
After confirmation, link the person to the story and suggest one follow-up question about them.

example.transcript_excerpt: My grandmother Linda always baked bread on Saturdays.
example.suggestion: Ene mentioned her grandmother Linda. Add Linda to the family tree as Ene's grandmother?
example.follow_up_question: What else do you remember about your grandmother Linda?

tree_expansion.non_relatives: Friends, neighbours and colleagues are tagged as people in the story, not added to the tree.

follow_up_prompts: What did it look, sound or smell like?
How did you feel right then?

generation_context.1: Ene (1957) and Kalmer (1958): grew up in Soviet Estonia in the 1960s, young adults in the 1970s, raised four children through the Singing Revolution, independence in 1991 and the 1990s.
generation_context.2: Jaanika, Marju, Liis, Tanel and partners Martin and Mathis (born 1984 to 1992): childhood in late Soviet times or the 1990s, grew up alongside Estonia's independence and the arrival of the internet; several have lived or studied abroad. Now in their 30s and 40s, some raising children.
generation_context.3: Grandchildren Lili-Marleen (12), Elisabeth (8), Liv (6), Iris (4), Artur (2): the older two can answer simple questions with help; stories about the younger ones are told by their parents and grandparents.

shared_meaning: shared = true means a memory many people may have lived. Ask everyone who was there for their own version, separately, so no one hears another version first.
